qt: to the Commission César Luena (S&D) Subject:

The European mink is the mammal most at risk of extinction on our continent, with its range having shrunk by more than 95% since the mid-19th century. Globally, only three sub-populations survive: in north-west and south-east Europe and in western Europe. Since 2018, the European mink has been listed as critically endangered and included in the Spanish Catalogue of Endangered Species as being ‘at risk of extinction’. A recent study found the mink population in Spain to number only 142 animals. The main conservation measures have focused on captive breeding and the fight against American mink, an invasive species which is one of its main threats. A captive breeding centre is currently being set up at the Finca Ribavellosa estate, which will be key to its survival. In light of the above: 1.
What support can the Commission provide to help make the national centre for the captive breeding of European mink at Ribavellosa operational?
Does the Commission not believe that the preservation of European mink should be prioritised under EU programmes such as LIFE?
What specific measures will the Commission take to ensure the survival of European mink?
at: (English version) to the Commission César Luena (S&D) (24 April 2024) Subject: Survival of the European mink The European mink is the mammal most at risk of extinction on our continent, with its range having shrunk by more than 95% since the mid-19th century. Globally, only three sub-populations survive: in north-west and south-east Europe and in western Europe. Since 2018, the European mink has been listed as critically endangered and included in the Spanish Catalogue of Endangered Species as being ‘at risk of extinction’. A recent study found the mink population in Spain to number only 142 animals. The main conservation measures have focused on captive breeding and the fight against American mink, an invasive species which is one of its main threats. A captive breeding centre is currently being set up at the Finca Ribavellosa estate, which will be key to its survival. In light of the above: 1.
What support can the Commission provide to help make the national centre for the captive breeding of European mink at Ribavellosa operational?

What specific measures will the Commission take to ensure the survival of European mink?

(13 June 2024) 1. EU financial support for a captive breeding centre to boost the Spanish population of the European mink could be provided through the EU programme for the environment and climate action (LIFE) (1) in line with the call for proposals currently underway (2). Past and ongoing LIFE projects have already contributed to improve the status of this species (3). 2. The European mink is (1) a priority species in Annex II of the Habitats Directive (4), (2) in a critically endangered status according to the EU red list of mammals and (3) in an unfavourable-bad status with declining trends as reported by Spain in the national report submitted under Article 17 of the Habitats Directive. This implies that the European mink is already considered as a top priority for funding under the LIFE nature and biodiversity sub-programme, and that a project targeting the species is entitled to the highest possible EU co-funding rate for LIFE Standard Action grants, namely 75%. 3. In addition to the measures already taken as indicated above, the Commission recalls that the American Mink, which is a non-native competitor of European minks, has been proposed for listing under Regulation 1143/2014 (5) in 2016. However, the species was not included in the list due to insufficient support by Member States. An updated risk assessment is currently being finalised, and this species may be proposed for the next update of the list in 2025.
